content_voiceover: This is the pivotal phase III trial for valoctocogene roxaparvovec, the AAV5-based gene therapy for severe hemophilia A, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. This was an open-label, single-group study enrolling 134 adult men with severe hemophilia A, defined as factor VIII activity of one international unit per deciliter or less. Look at the three panels. The left panel tracks factor VIII activity over 52 weeks after a single infusion, and you can see levels rise from essentially undetectable to a durable range in the twenties to fifties, with a mean increase of about 42 international units per deciliter, highly statistically significant. The middle panel shows treated bleeding episodes dropping from a baseline annualized rate of 4.8 down to just 0.8, an 83.8% reduction. The right panel shows factor VIII infusions plummeting from about 136 per year at baseline to essentially 2 per year after treatment, a 98.6% reduction, which really captures the treatment burden relief this therapy offers. The tradeoff, noted at the bottom, is that 16.4% of patients experienced serious adverse events, which is an important counterpoint for any board question about gene therapy safety.
keypoints: Single AAV5 infusion of valoctocogene roxaparvovec raised factor VIII activity from undetectable to mean increase of ~42 IU/dl
Treated bleeding episodes fell 83.8%, from 4.8 to 0.8 events per year
Factor VIII infusions fell 98.6%, from about 136 to about 2 per year
16.4% of patients had serious adverse events, a key safety caveat
keypoint_voiceover: Key trial numbers, this single gene therapy infusion for severe hemophilia A produced an 84% reduction in bleeding episodes and nearly eliminated the need for factor VIII infusions, but with serious adverse events in about one in six patients.
